title: Teen Invents Plant-Based Plastic That Eats Microplastics
summary: Microplastics are tiny bits of plastic that hide in oceans, soil, food, and even the air. They're so small that removing them is super hard. But 18-year-old Arya Satheesh from Ireland came up with a clever fix. She invented Eco Purge, a plant-based plastic that decomposes naturally — and while it breaks down, it also helps destroy microplastics already in the environment. Arya got interested in 2024 when she built a water-quality sensor for a science competition. Her device could find microplastics, but it couldn't remove them. So she started making Eco Purge. To do it, she needed two natural enzymes. Some companies wanted to sell them, but they cost too much. So Arya emailed Professor Kevin O'Connor at BiOrbic in Ireland. He got her the enzymes and let her use a university lab. By early 2026, she had a prototype. She tested it in soil, salt water, and fresh water for six weeks. At the end, both the microplastic and Eco Purge had decomposed. Her invention won the European regional title at The Earth Prize in May 2026, plus $12,500. "Science isn't just about understanding the world," she says. "It's about leaving it better than we found it."
why_it_matters: Microplastics can end up in the water you drink and the food you eat, so an invention that helps clean them up could make everyday life healthier for everyone — and it shows that a kid with a science-fair idea can start solving a really big problem.

background_read: Microplastics come from bigger plastic items that slowly break apart, and scientists have found them in oceans, rivers, and even in snow on high mountains.
Normal plastic can take hundreds of years to break down, which is why so much of it piles up in the environment instead of disappearing.
The Earth Prize (a competition that gives money and support to young people with ideas to help the planet) is one of several contests where student inventors can show their work.
Article_Structure: WHO: Arya Satheesh, an 18-year-old inventor from Ireland, helped by Professor Kevin O'Connor at BiOrbic, a research centre in Ireland.
WHAT: She invented Eco Purge, a plant-based plastic that decomposes naturally and also helps destroy microplastics already in the environment.
WHERE: In Ireland, where she tested her prototype in a university lab and then in soil, salt water, and fresh water.
WHY: Her first device could find microplastics but not remove them, so she built something that could clean them up while breaking down itself.

perspectives.description: Arya's story proves that students can do real science: she emailed a professor, got help, and won a big prize. It encourages other kids to try their own ideas.
A prototype that worked for six weeks in a lab is not the same as cleaning up a whole ocean. Making enough Eco Purge to help the planet could be slow and expensive.
Plastic pollution is a worldwide problem, and researchers and companies are testing many different fixes. Eco Purge is one promising idea among many that still needs to be tested at a bigger scale.
